title: Finance U5·W3 — Month-End Close, Cutoff and the GL-to-Trial-Balance Tie-Out
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the close is a control, not a chore

Everything in Units 4 and 5 so far assumed the numbers were complete and in the right period. The close is what makes that assumption true. A construction close has three jobs: get all the cost into the right period (cutoff), prove every balance-sheet account is real (reconciliation), and prove the reported statements tie to the ledger and the sub-ledgers (the tie-out). Skip any one and the WIP schedule — which depends entirely on complete, correctly periodized job cost — is wrong no matter how well the percent-complete formula is built.

The close calendar

A repeatable close is a calendar with named owners, not a heroic week. Meridian’s runs on business days relative to month end:

Meridian Building Group — close calendar
DayTaskOwner
−2Cutoff notice issued; PO and subcontract commitments frozen; field asked for work-in-place estimatesController
+1Payroll posted and burdened; AP entry cut off; bank feeds importedAP / payroll
+2Received-not-vouchered accrual booked; equipment and internal charges postedStaff accountant
+3Bank reconciliations complete; all balance-sheet reconciliations complete; clearing accounts proven to zeroStaff accountant
+4Job cost sub-ledger tied to GL; EAC updates approved in the job reviewController / PMs
+5WIP schedule built; reclass entry posted; statements drafted, reviewed and issuedController / CFO

Meridian’s close ran 14 business days before this calendar existed and runs 5 after. Speed is not the point — a close that takes three weeks produces information nobody can act on, and a management team that has stopped reading a report is worse off than one that never had it.

Cutoff — the accrual that makes construction different

The defining cutoff problem in construction is that work is performed long before it is invoiced. A subcontractor pours foundations the last week of September and submits a pay application on October 6. If Meridian recognizes revenue on cost-to-cost and the cost is not there, percent complete is understated, earned revenue is understated, and the job looks less complete than it is — on every open job, in the same direction, every month.

The fix is a received-not-vouchered accrual built from the field, not from the mail. At September 30, superintendents verified $214,600 of subcontract work in place; vouchered invoices totaled $178,900; the accrual is $35,700, reversed on October 1 as the actual invoices arrive.

Then test it. Meridian samples the first 15 invoices posted in October and checks service dates against the accrual: 3 invoices carried September service dates totaling $22,400, of which $19,600 was already captured. The uncaptured $2,800 is posted, and — more importantly — the pattern is investigated, because a systematic gap on one trade means the field verification is missing that trade every month. The mirror test runs backwards: sample large September postings and confirm the work was actually performed in September, not accrued twice.

Other cutoff points that bite: owner billings (a pay application dated October 3 for September work belongs in September billings), material deliveries (received on site September 29, invoiced October 8), payroll (a week straddling month end must be split by day, not by check date), and equipment and internal charges, which are journal entries nobody chases and so are the most commonly missed.

The tie-out

Three ties, in order, and none is optional:

  1. The trial balance foots and balances. Total debits equal total credits.
  2. GL detail sums to the trial balance for every account. A trial balance is a summary of the detail; if it disagrees with the detail, the export is filtered, dated wrong, or excluding a journal source.
  3. Every sub-ledger ties to its control account.
Meridian — sub-ledger to control account tie at September 30
Sub-ledgerSub-ledger totalGL controlDifference
AP aging$1,482,940$1,482,940—
AR aging$2,317,455$2,331,455$14,000
Job cost inception-to-date$8,946,120$8,946,120—
Retainage payable detail$618,300$618,300—

The $14,000 is an unapplied cash receipt posted to the GL control account but never applied in the receivables sub-ledger. It is named, aged and corrected — not carried as “immaterial.” A difference you tolerate this month is a difference you will not recognize as new next month.

Then the zero-balance proofs. Clearing and suspense accounts exist to hold transactions in flight, and every one of them must read $0.00 at the close, in total. Account 1195 — Interentity Transfer Clearing:

  • Meridian Building Group   $182,400 Dr
  • Riverton Partners   $(176,900) Cr
  • Northstar Services   $(5,500) Cr
  • Net $0.00 — proven.

A clearing account that does not net to zero is an unposted or miscoded leg, and Unit 6 Week 1 explains why the answer is never to eliminate it on a consolidation worksheet.

The trap: a trial balance that suppresses zero-balance accounts

Here is the defect that manufactures work out of nothing, and it is entirely a data-handling problem rather than an accounting one. Meridian’s ledger export omits any account with a zero balance in the period. August’s trial balance therefore has 312 rows and September’s has 298, because 14 accounts that carried balances in August went to zero in September.

The analyst builds the month-over-month variance workbook by pasting the two exports side by side and subtracting row from row. Every row is aligned until the first suppressed account, and every row after it is off by one — then by two, then by three, cascading down the sheet.

Concretely: account 5340 Equipment Rental held $46,800 in August and $0.00 in September, so it vanished from the September export. At that row the workbook now compares August’s 5340 ($46,800) against September’s next account, 5350 Small Tools ($9,240), and reports a $37,560 variance that describes no real event. The workbook flagged 56 accounts above the $25,000 review threshold. Every one was an artifact of misalignment. The four variances that were genuinely worth explaining did not appear on the list at all, because they had been shifted into rows that happened to look quiet.

This trap is dangerous specifically because it looks like diligence. Someone produces 56 exceptions, a team spends a week clearing them, everyone concludes the ledger was fine, and the real movements were never examined. Four defenses, all cheap:

  1. Never join on row position. Join on the account number, with an exact string match — not a fuzzy match, not the account name, which gets renamed and re-spelled.
  2. Use a full outer join and zero-fill. Accounts in either period must appear, with a missing side treated as $0.00. That converts the 5340 case into what it actually is: a real $46,800 decrease, correctly flagged.
  3. Reconcile the account population. 312 August rows minus 14 accounts that went to zero equals 298 September rows. If that arithmetic does not close, the export changed in a way you have not accounted for.
  4. Foot both exports to the GL control totals before either is used. A trial balance that does not foot to the ledger is not a trial balance.

The same family of defect appears in a GL export whose last column is labeled Ending Balance but is period activity — a mix that is especially easy to miss because it is correct for income-statement accounts and wrong for balance-sheet accounts in the same file. Unit 4 Week 1 showed what that does to a percent-complete calculation. The rule generalizes: prove what a column contains before you subtract with it.

Materiality, passed adjustments and the review

Not every difference gets posted. Meridian sets a posting threshold of $2,500 individually, with an aggregate cap of $12,500 across all passed items, tracked on a summary of unadjusted differences that carries forward. Two rules keep this honest. Passed items are listed, not forgotten, so the aggregate can be evaluated and so a difference that recurs in the same direction every month is recognized as a systematic error rather than noise. And a threshold applies to errors, never to unreconciled balances — “the account is off by $1,900, which is below the threshold” is not a reconciliation; it is an unreconciled account with a smaller number attached.

Finally, every reconciliation carries a preparer and a reviewer, and the reviewer’s signature means the supporting detail was examined, not that the sheet was opened. Self-reviewed reconciliations are the single most common control deficiency reported in a small accounting department, and in a three-person office the compensating control is that the CFO reviews the schedules the controller prepares.

CMA bridge

This is Part 1-E Internal Controls almost line for line: control activities, segregation of preparation from review, reconciliation as a detective control, cutoff procedures, and the completeness assertion. The tie-out chain is Part 1-A (how statements are derived from a ledger) and the variance workbook failure is Part 1-F technology and analytics — data quality, join keys, and why an analysis can be arithmetically perfect and completely wrong.

Practice and recap

  1. Run the close on a calendar with named owners and fixed days. Meridian went from 14 business days to 5.
  2. Accrue received-not-vouchered cost from field verification: $214,600 verified less $178,900 vouchered = $35,700. Then test it against October postings and investigate the pattern, not just the amount.
  3. Tie in order: TB balances, GL detail sums to TB, every sub-ledger ties to its control. Name every difference, including a $14,000 unapplied receipt.
  4. Prove every clearing and suspense account to $0.00 across all entities: $182,400 − $176,900 − $5,500 = $0.00.
  5. Join period-over-period data on the ACCOUNT NUMBER with a full outer join and zero-fill. Row-position joins on a zero-suppressing export produced 56 false positives and hid the 4 real ones.

Recap: the close makes complete, correctly periodized cost possible, which is what the whole WIP machinery rests on; cutoff in construction means accruing work in place from the field rather than waiting for invoices; the tie-out is a fixed chain from trial balance to GL detail to every sub-ledger with clearing accounts proven to zero; and the most expensive close-analysis mistake is not arithmetic but a join — a trial balance that suppresses zero-balance accounts will manufacture dozens of false variances and conceal the real ones unless you join on account number and zero-fill.

flashcards.front: The three jobs of a construction close
flashcards.back: (1) Cutoff — all cost in the right period. (2) Reconciliation — every balance-sheet account proven real. (3) Tie-out — statements tie to the GL and every sub-ledger. The WIP schedule depends entirely on complete, correctly periodized job cost.

Built from FIELD-verified work in place, not from invoices received. Sept 30: $214,600 verified − $178,900 vouchered = $35,700 accrued, reversed Oct 1. Missing it understates cost, % complete and earned revenue on every open job in the same direction.

Sample the first invoices posted in the new month and check service dates: 3 of 15 carried September dates totaling $22,400, of which $19,600 was accrued — post the $2,800 gap AND investigate why that trade is missed every month.

(1) TB foots and balances. (2) GL detail sums to the TB for every account. (3) Every sub-ledger (AP, AR, job cost, retainage, fixed assets, payroll) ties to its control account. Name every difference — a $14,000 unapplied receipt is an error, not immateriality.

Every clearing and suspense account must read $0.00 in total at close. Account 1195: MBG $182,400 Dr, Riverton $(176,900), Northstar $(5,500) = $0.00. A non-zero clearing balance is an unposted or miscoded leg.

flashcards.front: Trap — a TB that suppresses zero-balance accounts
flashcards.back: August 312 rows, September 298 rows because 14 accounts went to zero. Pasting the exports side by side and subtracting row-from-row misaligns everything after the first suppressed account — 56 flagged variances, all artifacts, and the 4 real ones invisible.

Account 5340 Equipment Rental: $46,800 in August, $0.00 (suppressed) in September. The workbook compares $46,800 against the NEXT account, 5350 Small Tools at $9,240, and reports a $37,560 'variance' describing no real event.

flashcards.front: Four defenses against the join defect
flashcards.back: (1) Join on ACCOUNT NUMBER, exact match — never row position, never account name. (2) Full outer join, zero-fill the missing side. (3) Reconcile the account population: 312 − 14 = 298. (4) Foot both exports to the GL control totals before using either.

quiz.title: Month-End Close, Cutoff and the Tie-Out

questions.q: Superintendents verified $214,600 of subcontract work in place at September 30; vouchered invoices totaled $178,900. The received-not-vouchered accrual is:
choices: $35,700, reversed October 1
$0 — accrue only when invoices arrive
questions.explain: $214,600 − $178,900 = $35,700. Waiting for invoices understates cost, percent complete and earned revenue on every open job, always in the same direction.

questions.q: August's trial balance export has 312 rows and September's has 298 because zero-balance accounts are suppressed. A variance workbook built by pasting the two side by side and subtracting row from row will:
choices: Misalign every row after the first suppressed account, manufacturing false variances
Correctly report all variances
Only affect income-statement accounts
Fail to foot, revealing the problem immediately
questions.explain: Suppression shifts the second column upward from the first missing account onward. The workbook still foots and still looks like real analysis — that is what makes it dangerous.

questions.q: Account 5340 Equipment Rental held $46,800 in August and $0.00 in September, so it is suppressed. The misaligned workbook compares it to 5350 Small Tools at $9,240 and reports a variance of:
choices: $37,560 — describing no real event
$46,800 — the true decrease
questions.explain: $46,800 − $9,240 = $37,560, an artifact. The real fact — equipment rental fell $46,800 to zero — is never flagged as itself.

questions.q: The correct way to build a period-over-period account variance analysis is to:
choices: Full outer join on exact account number, treating a missing side as $0.00
Inner join on account name
Sort both exports and compare by row position
Compare only accounts present in both periods
questions.explain: Row position and account names both break. A full outer join on the account number with zero-fill converts the suppressed 5340 into a correctly flagged $46,800 decrease.

questions.q: Account 1195 Interentity Transfer Clearing shows $182,400 Dr at Meridian, $(176,900) at Riverton and $(5,500) at Northstar. This is:
choices: Correct — the clearing account nets to $0.00 across the entities
An error of $182,400 at Meridian
An intercompany balance requiring elimination
An unrecorded receivable
questions.explain: $182,400 − $176,900 − $5,500 = $0.00. A clearing account is proven by netting to zero across all entities; only a non-zero net is an error.

questions.q: A staff accountant writes 'account is off by $1,900, below the $2,500 threshold' on a reconciliation. This is:
choices: Not a reconciliation — a posting threshold applies to identified errors, not to unreconciled balances
Acceptable, since the amount is immaterial
Acceptable if the reviewer signs it
Correct only if the aggregate stays under $12,500
questions.explain: A threshold lets you decline to POST a known, identified error. An unexplained difference is an unreconciled account regardless of size.

questions.q: The AR aging totals $2,317,455 and the GL control account shows $2,331,455. The correct treatment of the $14,000 is to:
choices: Identify it — here, an unapplied cash receipt — and correct it
Adjust the sub-ledger to the GL
Adjust the GL to the sub-ledger
Carry it forward as an immaterial reconciling item
questions.explain: A difference you tolerate this month is one you will not recognize as new next month. Name it, then correct the side that is wrong.
